Historical Background of Murshidabad Murshidabad occupies a distinguished place in India’s history. During the early eighteenth century, it emerged as one of the wealthiest and most influential cities in Asia. Situated along the banks of the Bhagirathi River, the city became the administrative, commercial, and cultural centre of Bengal under the Nawabs. Originally known as Makhsudabad, the city was renamed Murshidabad in honour of Murshid Quli Khan, who transferred the capital of Bengal from Dhaka in 1704. Under his leadership, Murshidabad rapidly evolved into a thriving political and economic powerhouse. Merchants from Britain, France, Holland, Armenia, and other parts of the world established trading settlements here, drawn by Bengal’s flourishing silk, muslin, and textile industries. The city reached its zenith during the reigns of successive Nawabs, particularly Alivardi Khan and his grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah. Magnificent palaces, mosques, gardens, caravanserais, and public buildings reflected the immense wealth generated through trade and agriculture. However, Murshidabad’s fortunes changed dramatically after the Battle of Plassey in 1757, when Siraj-ud-Daulah was defeated by the British East India Company under Robert Clive. This pivotal event marked the beginning of British political dominance in India and forever altered the course of the nation’s history. Although Kolkata eventually replaced Murshidabad as the capital of British Bengal, the city retained its aristocratic character. The Nawabs continued to patronise art, architecture, education, and culture, leaving behind an extraordinary legacy visible in the city’s splendid monuments today. Visitors to Murshidabad can still admire grand palaces, impressive mosques, elegant gardens, merchant mansions, royal cemeteries, and colonial buildings that together narrate more than three centuries of Bengal’s remarkable past. Overnight Stay: Jalchhabi Hotel and Resort Day 2 – Discover the Glorious Heritage of the Nawabs After breakfast, begin an immersive exploration of Murshidabad’s remarkable monuments, where every palace, mosque, and gateway tells the story of Bengal’s royal past. Khosbagh (Garden of Happiness) Located on the western bank of the Bhagirathi River, Khosbagh is one of Murshidabad’s most revered historical sites. Surrounded by high walls and tranquil gardens, this peaceful cemetery serves as the final resting place of several members of the Nawab family, including Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah, the last independent Nawab of Bengal, and his grandfather Nawab Alivardi Khan. The atmosphere here is serene and reflective, inviting visitors to pause and contemplate one of the most dramatic chapters in Indian history. Following Siraj-ud-Daulah’s defeat at the Battle of Plassey in 1757, Bengal entered a new era under British rule. His simple grave remains an enduring reminder of the turning point that changed the course of India’s history. The beautifully maintained gardens and riverside setting add to the site’s timeless charm, making it one of the most meaningful places to visit in Murshidabad. Nizamat Imambara Standing opposite Hazarduari Palace, the magnificent Nizamat Imambara is among the largest Shia congregation halls in India. The present structure was commissioned by Nawab Nazim Mansur Ali Khan Feradun Jah after the earlier building was destroyed by fire in 1846. Stretching over 600 feet in length, the Imambara is an architectural masterpiece characterised by elegant arcades, graceful domes, expansive courtyards, and long colonnaded corridors. During the Islamic month of Muharram, thousands of devotees gather here to commemorate the martyrdom of Imam Hussain through solemn religious ceremonies. The Imambara also houses sacred relics and beautifully decorated prayer halls, reflecting the spiritual traditions of Murshidabad’s Nawabi rulers. Hazarduari Palace No visit to Murshidabad is complete without exploring the magnificent Hazarduari Palace, undoubtedly the city’s most iconic landmark. Constructed between 1829 and 1837 under the supervision of British architect Colonel Duncan MacLeod, the palace was commissioned by Nawab Nazim Humayun Jah. Its name literally means “The Palace of One Thousand Doors.” Interestingly, only about one hundred of these doors are functional, while the remainder were cleverly designed as false doors to confuse intruders and enhance the palace’s grandeur. Designed in an elegant Italian-Greek style, the three-storey palace houses an outstanding museum managed by the Archaeological Survey of India. Visitors can admire priceless collections of royal furniture, chandeliers, paintings, manuscripts, marble sculptures, antique clocks, European mirrors, ivory artefacts, rare weapons, and portraits of the Nawabs. The palace beautifully illustrates the blend of Mughal traditions and European architectural influences that characterised nineteenth-century Bengal. Yellow Mosque (Zurud Mosque) Often overlooked by casual visitors, the elegant Yellow Mosque, also known as the Zurud Mosque, is a charming example of late Nawabi architecture. Built using distinctive yellow-coloured plaster, the mosque features graceful domes, delicate arches, decorative floral motifs, and beautifully proportioned minarets. Despite its relatively modest size, the mosque demonstrates the refinement and artistic taste of Murshidabad’s Nawabi builders. Its peaceful surroundings make it an ideal stop for those interested in Islamic architecture and photography. Bachhawali Tope (The Great Cannon) Near Hazarduari Palace stands the enormous Bachhawali Tope, one of the largest cannons ever cast in the Indian subcontinent. Measuring nearly eighteen feet in length and weighing approximately seven tonnes, the cannon was manufactured during the reign of Nawab Sarfaraz Khan by skilled craftsmen under the supervision of Janardan Karmakar, a renowned Bengali metallurgist. Legend has it that the thunderous sound produced by firing the cannon was so powerful that it caused miscarriages among pregnant women in the surrounding area. This popular folklore gave rise to its name, “Bachhawali,” meaning “child-bearing.” Although never extensively used in warfare, the cannon remains an impressive symbol of Murshidabad’s military history and engineering expertise. Tripolia Gate The historic Tripolia Gate once served as the grand ceremonial entrance to the Nawabs’ palace complex. Built with three elegant arches, the gate symbolised the power and prestige of the Murshidabad court. Royal processions, military parades, and distinguished guests entered through this impressive gateway, making it one of the city’s most significant architectural landmarks during the Nawabi period. Today, the gate continues to stand as a reminder of Murshidabad’s glorious royal heritage and offers excellent photographic opportunities. Wasif Manzil Situated beside the Bhagirathi River, the elegant Wasif Manzil, also known as the New Palace, was built by Nawab Wasif Ali Mirza during the late nineteenth century after the original palace suffered earthquake damage. Designed in a European classical style, the palace features graceful Corinthian columns, sweeping staircases, beautifully landscaped gardens, and spacious halls that once hosted royal gatherings. Although smaller than Hazarduari Palace, Wasif Manzil reflects the continued influence of European architecture on the later Nawabs while preserving the regal elegance associated with Murshidabad’s aristocracy. Namak Haram Deorhi The Namak Haram Deorhi, meaning the “Gate of the Traitor,” occupies a unique place in Indian history. Tradition associates this site with the betrayal of Nawab Siraj-ud-Daulah following the Battle of Plassey. Historical accounts suggest that Siraj-ud-Daulah was brought here after his capture before being executed on the orders of Mir Jafar’s son, Miran. While historians continue to debate certain details surrounding these events, the site has become a powerful symbol of political intrigue, betrayal, and the dramatic fall of Bengal’s last independent Nawab. Standing here offers visitors a poignant reminder of one of the defining moments in India’s colonial history. Following a full day of exploration, return to Jalchhabi Hotel and Resort for a relaxing evening and overnight stay. Day 3 – Mosques, Merchant Mansions and Colonial Heritage After breakfast, continue your exploration of Murshidabad’s remarkable religious monuments and aristocratic residences before returning to Kolkata. Katra Masjid One of Murshidabad’s oldest and most significant monuments, Katra Masjid was commissioned by Murshid Quli Khan, the founder of Murshidabad, in 1724. Designed as both a mosque and an Islamic educational institution (madrasa), the complex once accommodated hundreds of students studying theology and Islamic law. The mosque originally featured four towering minarets, though only two survive today following earthquake damage. Its massive courtyard, impressive staircases, thick walls, and elegant arches demonstrate the strength and simplicity of early eighteenth-century Mughal architecture. Murshid Quli Khan himself requested to be buried beneath the entrance steps so that worshippers would walk over his grave as a mark of humility—a wish that was honoured after his death. Madina Mosque Located within the Katra Masjid complex, the small yet spiritually significant Madina Mosque is believed to contain bricks or sacred earth brought from Medina in Saudi Arabia. The mosque remains an important pilgrimage site for many devotees and beautifully complements the larger Katra Masjid through its simple yet elegant architectural style. Its religious importance makes it one of Murshidabad’s cherished spiritual landmarks. House of Jagat Seth The House of Jagat Seth introduces visitors to one of the wealthiest banking families in eighteenth-century India. The Jagat Seths controlled enormous financial resources and played a major role in Bengal’s political affairs. Their banking empire financed rulers, merchants, and even European trading companies. Today, the museum displays fascinating collections of coins, banking documents, antique furniture, paintings, jewellery, and household objects that illustrate the immense prosperity enjoyed by this influential family. The house also provides valuable insight into the economic forces that shaped Bengal during the Nawabi era. Kathgola Palace Among Murshidabad’s finest heritage mansions, Kathgola Palace was built by the affluent Dugar family, prominent Jain merchants who prospered through trade. The palace combines European, Bengali, and classical architectural styles, featuring magnificent Corinthian columns, marble statues, elegant balconies, ornate interiors, and beautifully landscaped gardens. Within the estate, visitors can also explore the exquisite Jain Temple, decorative fountains, and peaceful courtyards. Kathgola Palace reflects the cosmopolitan nature of Murshidabad, where prosperous merchants from diverse communities contributed to the city’s cultural richness. Clock Tower of Murshidabad The elegant Clock Tower stands as a reminder of Murshidabad’s colonial period and its gradual transformation during the nineteenth century. Once serving as an important public timekeeper for residents and traders, the tower remains one of the city’s recognisable landmarks and provides an excellent backdrop for photographs before concluding your heritage tour. Architecture and Design of Murshidabad’s Heritage Monuments Murshidabad is a treasure trove of architectural diversity, where Mughal, Nawabi, Bengali, Persian, and European influences converge to create one of India’s most fascinating heritage landscapes. As the capital of Bengal during the eighteenth century, the city attracted skilled architects, artisans, craftsmen, and merchants from across the Indian subcontinent and beyond. Their collective expertise shaped the palaces, mosques, gateways, gardens, and mansions that continue to captivate visitors today. Indo-Islamic Elegance Many of Murshidabad’s religious monuments, including Katra Masjid, Madina Mosque, and Nizamat Imambara, display classic Indo-Islamic architectural elements. Graceful pointed arches, spacious courtyards, domes, minarets, and symmetrical layouts reflect Mughal design principles while incorporating local Bengali craftsmanship. Unlike the heavily ornamented Mughal monuments of North India, Murshidabad’s Islamic architecture often features restrained decoration, emphasizing elegant proportions and functional beauty. Decorative stucco work, floral motifs, intricate calligraphy, and finely crafted mihrabs demonstrate the artistic sophistication of the period. European Classical Influence During the nineteenth century, European architectural styles began to influence Murshidabad’s royal buildings. This is most evident in Hazarduari Palace and Wasif Manzil, where Greek and Italian Renaissance design elements blend seamlessly with the city’s Nawabi heritage. Visitors will notice: Grand Corinthian and Ionic columns Impressive porticos Wide ceremonial staircases Large arched windows Classical pediments Spacious halls with high ceilings Symmetrical façades These features reflect the close interaction between the Nawabs and British architects during the colonial period while preserving the city’s regal identity. Palaces Built for Grandeur Murshidabad’s palaces were more than royal residences—they were symbols of authority, diplomacy, and cultural refinement. The famous Hazarduari Palace, with its thousand doors and extensive museum collections, remains the finest example of royal architecture in eastern India. Similarly, Kathgola Palace illustrates the wealth and artistic taste of Murshidabad’s prosperous merchant community through its elegant gardens, marble statues, and beautifully decorated interiors. Even smaller structures such as Wasif Manzil reveal remarkable attention to proportion, landscape design, and architectural harmony. Fortifications and Ceremonial Gateways Structures like Tripolia Gate demonstrate the importance of ceremonial architecture within the Nawabi capital. These monumental gateways welcomed royal processions, distinguished visitors, and military parades, reinforcing the prestige of the ruling court. Meanwhile, defensive elements represented by the enormous Bachhawali Tope illustrate the military preparedness of the Nawabs during an era of political uncertainty. A Living Heritage City Unlike many historic capitals that survive only as archaeological ruins, Murshidabad remains a living heritage destination where religious ceremonies, local traditions, historic markets, and everyday life continue alongside centuries-old monuments. Walking through its streets offers visitors an immersive experience where history is not confined to museums but remains an integral part of the city’s cultural identity.
